contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Eleanor of Aquitaine was duchess of Aquitaine, queen of France, and queen of England, one of the most politically important women of the High Middle Ages. Her inheritance linked Poitiers and Aquitaine to the highest dynastic politics of France and England, and her marriages shaped the rivalry between the Capetians and the Angevin rulers.

She took part in crusading culture, court politics, rebellion, imprisonment, and diplomacy across a long life. Eleanor died in 1204 at Fontevraud Abbey, leaving a legacy as ruler, patron, dynastic mother, and a figure later romanticized in stories of courtly culture.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Eleanor was born around 1122, probably in or near Poitiers, into the ducal house of Aquitaine. Some traditions place her birth elsewhere in Aquitaine, so the exact birthplace should be treated cautiously.
As heiress to one of the richest principalities in western Europe, she grew up in a court connected to troubadour culture, lordship, religious patronage, and the politics of the Kingdom of France.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Eleanor of Aquitaine's personality has been distorted by centuries of legend, much of it hostile and gendered. Clerical chroniclers of her own day, uneasy with a woman who wielded real power, circulated stories of scandal during the Second Crusade and presented her independence as waywardness. Modern historians treat these accounts cautiously: they reveal more about anxieties over female authority than about Eleanor herself.

What the record more securely supports is a woman of formidable political intelligence and stamina. She held Aquitaine in her own right, survived the annulment of one royal marriage and the long imprisonment that followed her support for her sons' revolt against Henry II, and re-emerged in old age as an active power-broker for Richard the Lionheart and John. Her endurance through decades of confinement and her decisive interventions in the succession show patience, resilience, and a refusal to be sidelined.

Later tradition romanticised her as the queen of courtly love, presiding over "courts of love" in Poitiers — a picture that owes more to later literary imagination than to evidence. The vivid, scheming, glamorous Eleanor of legend should be held at arm's length; the politically tenacious and unusually long-lived duchess-queen is the figure the sources actually sustain.

contentSections.title: As queen of France and England
paragraphs: Eleanor first became queen of France through her marriage to Louis VII, a union that brought Aquitaine into Capetian reach but ended in annulment. Her later marriage to Henry II connected Aquitaine to the Angevin world and made her queen of England.

She supported her sons during revolt against Henry II and spent years under restraint, but she returned to public power after Richard the Lionheart became king. In old age she remained a formidable political actor, helping secure dynastic interests between England, France, and Aquitaine.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died at Fontevraud Abbey in 1204 after spending her final years in monastic retirement and dynastic politics.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Eleanor is remembered as one of the most influential aristocratic women of medieval Europe. Her reputation has often been romanticized, especially in modern retellings of courtly love and royal intrigue, but her political importance was real.
Her life reveals the power of inheritance, marriage, lordship, and maternal diplomacy in a world where queenship could shape the fate of kingdoms even when formal sovereignty was contested.

timeline.title: Becomes Duchess of Aquitaine
timeline.description: Inherits Aquitaine after the death of her father, William X.

timeline.title: Marries Louis VII of France
timeline.description: Becomes queen consort of France through marriage.

timeline.title: Participates in the Second Crusade
timeline.description: Travels east with Louis VII during the crusade.

timeline.title: Marries Henry Plantagenet
timeline.description: After annulment from Louis VII, marries the future Henry II of England.

timeline.title: Supports revolt against Henry II
timeline.description: Backs her sons in rebellion and is imprisoned afterward.

succession.note: Eleanor ruled Aquitaine in her own right; her queenships of France and England were as consort.

predecessor.note: Her father, who died on pilgrimage in 1137 leaving her the duchy

successor.note: On her death in 1204 the duchy passed to her surviving son, King John, and Philip II overran most of it
